newsitem.title: DUBAI: Aircraft makers vie for bigger slice of UAE deal.
newsitem.headline: Aircraft makers vie for bigger slice of UAE deal.

text.p: France's Dassault Aviation could clinch a major portion of a $6 billion warplane deal with Abu Dhabi if its U.S. competitor refuses to supply sophisticated complementary weapons, industry sources said on Sunday.
"The U.S. is more circumspect (than the French). For national security reasons they may not release certain attack weapons to other countries," one said.
"The French are flexible. If the Americans are not forthcoming it will work in favour of the French. The UAE wants the best technology, because technology is perishable," he said.

The UAE has officially told the United States of its interest in the F-16 Block 60 warplane, dropping the rival U.S. F-15 but keeping the French Rafale in the contest, official military sources said in August.
A senior UAE official said McDonnell Douglas Corp's F-15 was out of the contest for up to 80 warplanes, with the U.S.'s Lockheed Martin and Dassault still in the running.
Lockheed Martin said last month its F-16 was one of two aircraft selected by the oil-rich UAE as final candidates in the package, which could be the last of its size this century.
The firm said it had offered a range of F-16 configurations for UAE consideration during the evaluation process.
"The competition is still active and heated," another industry source who requested anonymity told Reuters.
"The UAE has not told Lockheed that it would win a major share of the deal," he added.
Dassault officials in Abu Dhabi would not comment.
Colonel Khalid Abdullah, deputy commander of the UAE air force, is due to meet U.S. military officials and defence contractors on November 15, another industry source said.
"They are still discussing specifications. There is no agreement yet on numbers and what kind of weapons would go along with the deal," the first source said.
"They are still in the toss up," he added.
The UAE has emerged as a key player in the multi-billion dollar international arms market. It is expected to make its final selection on the warplane deal within a few months.
The first source said the UAE was interested in the F-16 because it was less expensive and was seen as less of a threat to powerful non-Arab Iran which faces the UAE across the Gulf.

"The F-16 is an air-to-air defence plane. It is seen as less threatening to Iran. When you are a nation of 2.5 million people you don't want to buy a more offensive plane that could threaten a country of 60 million people," he said.
U.S. defence contractors, eyeing lucrative weapons deals, are hoping that Lockheed wins a large chunk of the deal.
"This would be good news for U.S. subcontractors who make complementary weapons such as sidewinder missiles and radar systems," said an official from a major U.S. weapons maker.
